name: Admission clerks in a hospital say they always follow the official admission form, but the analyst suspects that daily practice differs. The new system must also exchange data with the existing laboratory system. Which elicitation techniques fit these two needs best?

answers.body: A brainstorming session to collect as many ideas as possible about admissions.
answers.comment: L2, slide 3: Brainstorming generates ideas freely; it gives no evidence of actual working practice or of the lab interface.

answers.body: Reverse engineering and interface analysis of the laboratory system.
answers.comment: L2, slide 3: This technique studies existing systems and the systems the new one must connect to.

answers.body: Observation (job shadowing): watch the clerks at work to see what they actually do.
answers.comment: L2, slide 3: Observation reveals what users actually do, which often differs from what they say.

answers.body: A questionnaire sent to the clerks asking how they process admissions.
answers.comment: L2, slide 3: Questionnaires reach many people quickly but give shallow, self-reported answers, so they repeat what clerks say rather than what they do.

name: Three departments disagree about the requirements of a new booking system and a decision is needed soon. In addition, one key user cannot describe the screens she needs, and a manager has hidden concerns he does not voice in meetings. Which techniques fit?

answers.body: A one-on-one, open-ended interview with the manager.
answers.comment: L2, slide 3: Interviews give depth and are good at uncovering hidden needs.

answers.body: A facilitated workshop (e.g. JAD) with all three departments.
answers.comment: L2, slide 3: Workshops bring stakeholders together to agree on requirements quickly.

answers.body: Document analysis of current regulations to resolve the disagreement between departments.
answers.comment: L2, slide 3: Document analysis reviews manuals, regulations and forms; it does not bring stakeholders to an agreement.

answers.body: A mockup or prototype that the user can react to.
answers.comment: L2, slide 3: Prototyping lets users react to something concrete when they cannot describe it in the abstract.

answers.body: A large online survey to explore the manager's concerns in depth.
answers.comment: L2, slide 3: Surveys reach many users but give shallower answers, the opposite of what an in-depth exploration needs.

name: A ticketing project needs to describe: (1) how a ticket moves between reserved, paid and cancelled; (2) the wish "As a passenger I want to buy a ticket on my phone so that I avoid queues", with conditions for acceptance; (3) which actors interact with the system and how. Which pairings of need and technique are correct?

answers.body: (3) BPMN or activity diagram of internal data storage.
answers.comment: L2, slide 4: BPMN, flowcharts and activity diagrams show workflows; actor–system interaction is the job of use cases.

answers.body: (1) State diagram.
answers.comment: L2, slide 4: State diagrams show how an entity changes state over time.

answers.body: (1) Entity-relationship diagram.
answers.comment: L2, slide 4: ER and class diagrams show the information the system handles, not the life cycle of one entity.

answers.body: (2) User story with acceptance criteria.
answers.comment: L2, slide 4: User stories are short "As a … I want … so that …" statements with acceptance criteria.

answers.body: (3) Data flow diagram.
answers.comment: L2, slide 4: A DFD shows how data moves through a system; actor–system interactions are described by use cases and use case diagrams.

name: How are use case modeling and domain modeling combined in this course?

answers.body: Use cases should already fix the implementation and architecture before domain analysis starts.
answers.comment: L2, slide 5: Use cases capture functional requirements without any implementation or architecture details.

answers.body: Analysis patterns are applied mainly to the use case model.
answers.comment: L2, slide 5: Analysis patterns are applied to the data (domain) modeling part.

answers.body: Thinking about domain concepts drives discussion about the functional requirements.
answers.comment: L2, slide 6: The domain model helps a common understanding, and thinking about concepts drives discussion of requirements.

answers.body: Use cases capture functional requirements, but only as broader context needed for the data modeling.
answers.comment: L2, slide 5: Use case modeling is used only to provide the functional context that data modeling needs.

name: The documentation of a transport company contains the nouns driver, motorman (used for the same person as driver), licence number, tram, line, depot and depot address. Which decisions follow the entity-identification method?

answers.body: Add methods such as assignDriver() and database keys so the diagram is ready for implementation.
answers.comment: L2, slide 8: The diagram stays at a conceptual level: no methods and no design attributes.

answers.body: Keep each noun as its own entity so that nothing is lost.
answers.comment: L2, slide 8: The list is reduced by merging synonyms and removing property nouns.

answers.body: Merge driver and motorman into one entity, because they are synonyms.
answers.comment: L2, slide 8: Synonyms that describe the same thing are consolidated.

answers.body: Leave out Depot, which is an address rather than a person.
answers.comment: L2, slide 8: Entities may be people, processes, system components or any other noun that must be documented or stored.

answers.body: Treat licence number and depot address as attributes of Driver and Depot, not as entities.
answers.comment: L2, slide 8: Nouns that are attributes or properties of other nouns are removed from the entity list.

name: A first conceptual model links Driver and Vehicle. Drivers hold licences for some vehicle kinds, and they also drive particular vehicles. What should the analyst do next?

answers.body: Model "has licence" and "drives" as two separate, named associations with roles and multiplicities.
answers.comment: L2, slides 9–10: Relationships are named and given roles and multiplicities; the transport model keeps "has license" and "drives" apart.

answers.body: Use one unnamed association between Driver and Vehicle to cover both relationships at once.
answers.comment: L2, slides 9–10: Different relationships need their own names so that their purpose is clear.

answers.body: Ask when a driver is assigned to a vehicle, how permanent the assignment is and what must be remembered about it.
answers.comment: L2, slide 10: These context questions (creation, permanence, history, responsibility) clarify functional requirements.

answers.body: Postpone such questions to the implementation phase, when the exact behaviour will be known.
answers.comment: L2, slide 9: Although the domain model is static, it is used to clarify behaviour and functional requirements.

name: Which statements reflect the course's view of domain models as living documentation?

answers.body: It should contain only as much information as is useful to the people involved.
answers.comment: L2, slide 11: Domain models are conversational and provide only as much information as is useful.

answers.body: Once approved, the domain model should be frozen to protect the shared understanding.
answers.comment: L2, slide 11: Shared understanding comes from keeping the model up to date, not from freezing it.

answers.body: Storing domain knowledge as AI-agent skills and constraints removes the need for iterative domain reasoning.
answers.comment: L2, slide 11: Knowledge can be stored this way, but building it still requires iterative reasoning, otherwise agents produce nonsense.

answers.body: A domain model is never done and never exhaustive; it is refined as understanding grows.
answers.comment: L2, slide 11: Domain models are living documents, continually refined, never done and never exhaustive.

name: Why use analysis patterns in domain modeling, even when an LLM can draft the model?

answers.body: Many concepts recur across domains, and well-documented patterns save reinventing them from scratch.
answers.comment: L2, slide 12: Recurring, domain-independent concepts can be described by well-documented guidelines instead of reinventing the wheel.

answers.body: A pattern is the final, correct model that should be copied unchanged.
answers.comment: L2, slide 20: Models are not right or wrong, only more or less useful; a pattern is a starting point, not a destination.

answers.body: An LLM already chooses suitable patterns by itself, so pattern knowledge matters mainly when drawing by hand.
answers.comment: L2, slides 13 and 16: The LLM answers the question it was asked; without pattern vocabulary it produces an average schema.

answers.body: Pattern vocabulary is needed both to prompt the LLM and to review its result.
answers.comment: L2, slide 13: You still need patterns to drive AI agents efficiently and to check their results (drive, generate, review).

name: An information system must (a) record who is responsible to whom between employees and organisational units, (b) store patients' blood pressure with units, and (c) track how goods and money move between warehouses and accounts. Which Fowler pattern collections match these concerns?

answers.body: (a) Accountability.
answers.comment: L2, slide 21: Accountability covers organisational structure and responsibilities.

answers.body: (a) Referring to Objects.
answers.comment: L2, slide 21: Referring to Objects is about identifying objects, not about responsibilities between parties.

answers.body: (c) Planning of stock movements.
answers.comment: L2, slide 21: Planning covers schedules and protocols for repetitive plans; movements between "pots" of resources are Inventory and Accounting.

answers.body: (c) Inventory and Accounting.
answers.comment: L2, slide 21: Inventory and Accounting covers cash flow and inventorying.

answers.body: (b) Observations and Measurements.
answers.comment: L2, slide 21: This collection is about measured values.

name: A city transport company asked an LLM for a data model. Model A: Depot employs 0..* Drivers, each Driver works at exactly 1 Depot (a fixed depot reference), and nothing is dated. Model B: Party, Accountability with an AccountabilityType and a TimePeriod. Three months later a new requirement arrives: "From January a driver may be temporarily assigned to a second depot, and when an accident occurs we must know who was responsible for that driver at that moment." Which conclusions are correct?

answers.body: For a company that never reorganises and never audits, Model A is the better choice because it is simpler.
answers.comment: L2, slide 16: The slide states this explicitly; Model B is heavier and harder to read.

answers.body: A short, vague prompt is enough for the LLM to choose Model B on its own.
answers.comment: L2, slide 16: A vague prompt gets the internet-average schema; choosing patterns and instructing the LLM precisely is the designer's skill.

answers.body: After a migration, Model A can rebuild the assignment history from before January.
answers.comment: L2, slide 16: That history is lost in Model A because it was never recorded; in Model B it is already there via TimePeriod.

answers.body: Model B is better in every situation, whatever the business needs.
answers.comment: L2, slide 16: Usefulness depends on the business; for a stable, unaudited company the simple model wins.

answers.body: In Model B the new requirement is a data change: one new AccountabilityType instance.
answers.comment: L2, slide 16: Model B needs only a new AccountabilityType instance; Model A needs a new table, a migration and a deprecated depot_id.

name: A reviewer finds the following defects in an LLM-generated domain model. Which repairs match the defect?

answers.body: Relationships look permanent and nothing says what was true in March → use TimePeriod on Accountability, Dual Time Record or Proposed vs. Implemented Action.
answers.comment: L2, slide 17: These are the remedies listed for missing temporal changes.

answers.body: People and companies end up as one table client(name, address, is_company) → add more boolean flags so each kind of client fits the same table.
answers.comment: L2, slides 17 and 26: This is the generic-CRUD failure itself; the repair is an abstract structure such as Party, Accountability or Observation.

answers.body: Temporal information is missing → rename the classes with precise domain terms and keep the permanent associations.
answers.comment: L2, slide 17: Renaming adds no time periods and does not separate when something happened from when it was recorded.

answers.body: Rules are hard-coded in the schema, so a new value needs a schema change → separate knowledge-level types (e.g. AccountabilityType, PhenomenonType) from operational entities.
answers.comment: L2, slide 17: Flattening of abstraction is repaired by distinguishing conceptual (knowledge) and operational entities.

name: An LLM generated a class Organization with a recursive association: <TT>parent</TT> with multiplicity 1 and <TT>children</TT> with multiplicity *. The brief says: "Associated Coffee Makers is the top organisation; its departments are sales and purchasing; sales has Boston and London offices." How should you check the model, and what do you find?

answers.body: Accept the model unchanged; its class names match the nouns of the brief.
answers.comment: L2, slide 18: A confident-looking schema can silently fail to cover a requirement; there is no error or warning.

answers.body: Apply a further analysis pattern such as Organization Structure, which guarantees that no requirement is missed.
answers.comment: L2, slide 18: No pattern fixes silent incompleteness; only testing with instances does.

answers.body: Write down requirements from the brief and try to build an object diagram that satisfies each one.
answers.comment: L2, slide 18: You must test the model, not read it; the requirement that cannot be instantiated is the gap.

answers.body: The top organisation cannot be instantiated, because every Organization must have exactly one parent; parent should be 0..1.
answers.comment: L2, slide 18: The slide crosses out the extra parent object that multiplicity 1 would demand above the top organisation.

name: Class ConversionRatio has an association to class Number, with exactly one Number per ConversionRatio. Which UML notations express the same information?

answers.body: Both the attribute <TT>ratio: Number</TT> and the association drawn together, read as one and the same value.
answers.comment: L2, slide 22: The third drawing shows attribute and association at once and is also marked as equal; they are two views of one value.

answers.body: Both the attribute and the association, read as two independent numbers stored in ConversionRatio.
answers.comment: L2, slide 22: The redundant drawing does not add a second value; it shows the same single Number twice.

answers.body: An attribute <TT>ratio: Number</TT> in ConversionRatio, with no association line.
answers.comment: L2, slide 22: The slide marks the association form and the attribute form as equal.

answers.body: Neither attribute nor association; the ratio is derived from the two units.
answers.comment: L2, slide 22: All equal notations keep the Number value; dropping it loses information.

name: A system handles people and companies. When is the Party pattern justified, and how is it applied?

answers.body: Whenever two classes share an attribute name such as <TT>name</TT>, they have to be merged into Party.
answers.comment: L2, slide 26: If people and companies do not share behaviour, keeping them separate is fine.

answers.body: Shared context (e.g. address, orders) is linked to Party, while context specific to one subtype stays on that subtype.
answers.comment: L2, slide 27: Common context goes to Party, specific context (e.g. employees of a company) to the specific term.

answers.body: If people and companies share behaviour, e.g. orders for either, a common Party supertype gives that shared context a place.
answers.comment: L2, slide 26: The key question is whether people and companies share behaviour; if they do, they need a common context.

answers.body: Party is a synonym for a natural person, so organisational units stay outside it and get their own hierarchy.
answers.comment: L2, slide 27: Party unifies individuals and organisational units (e.g. a teacher and a faculty) involved in mutual responsibility.

name: Sales offices belong to divisions, divisions to regions and regions to an operating unit. Instead of a fixed chain of associations OperatingUnit–Region–Division–SalesOffice, the Organization Hierarchies pattern uses Organization with a recursive association (<TT>parent</TT> 0..1, <TT>subsidiary</TT> 0..*) and the subtypes OperatingUnit, Region, Division and SalesOffice. What makes this version more flexible?

answers.body: The recursive version can no longer say which kinds of unit exist; all units are plain Organization objects.
answers.comment: L2, slides 30–31: The subtypes OperatingUnit, Region, Division and SalesOffice remain in the model.

answers.body: Each unit may have several parents, which is what makes the hierarchy flexible.
answers.comment: L2, slide 30: The parent end has multiplicity 0..1, so a unit has at most one parent; flexibility comes from the recursive association and the subtypes.

answers.body: Unit kinds remain as subtypes, and rules such as "the parent of a SalesOffice is a Division" are kept as constraints on them.
answers.comment: L2, slides 30–31: Subtypes discuss which units exist and are a suitable place for constraints on the hierarchy.

answers.body: One recursive parent–subsidiary association replaces all the level-to-level associations as a reusable backbone.
answers.comment: L2, slides 29–30: The solution to rigid hierarchies is a recursive relationship on Organization.

name: In the flexible Organization Hierarchies model (Organization with recursive parent/subsidiary association and subtypes Division, SalesOffice, …), a Subdivision must now be inserted between Division and SalesOffice. What is expected?

answers.body: Replace the recursive association with a separate association for every pair of levels.
answers.comment: L2, slide 32: The recursive backbone stays; rebuilding level-to-level associations is what the pattern avoids.

answers.body: Keep the rule that a SalesOffice's parent is a Division, even though the new structure says Subdivision.
answers.comment: L2, slide 32: The rules must be adapted to the new structure.

answers.body: Check whether the request reflects a real reorganisation or just better understanding during analysis.
answers.comment: L2, slide 29: Such requests often arise from iterative clarification of requirements, not only from real change.

answers.body: Add only one Subdivision subclass and update the parent rules, which are not part of the data model itself.
answers.comment: L2, slide 32: The changes are: add one subclass and change rules that are not part of the data model.

name: A company has several parallel organisational hierarchies (e.g. sales and public relations), and their number may grow. Why model them with the Organization Structure pattern (an OrganizationStructure class with an OrganizationStructureType) instead of one more recursive association per hierarchy?

answers.body: Each OrganizationStructure object is an edge of the tree, which gives a place for its type and extra context such as a TimePeriod.
answers.comment: L2, slides 36–37: Reflexive associations provide no space for context, so the association is replaced by a class.

answers.body: A unit must report to the same parent in every hierarchy; the structure objects share one parent link per unit.
answers.comment: L2, slide 38: Each structure type has its own parent links, e.g. Brno reports to Moravia in Sale but to Central in PR.

answers.body: A new hierarchy is introduced by adding a new subclass of OrganizationStructureType, one per kind of hierarchy, each with its own constraints.
answers.comment: L2, slide 37: Hierarchy types such as sales and production are recorded as instances of OrganizationStructureType, not new classes.

answers.body: Separate recursive associations lead to an explosion of subtypes and constraints, and an unknown number of hierarchies cannot be modelled that way.
answers.comment: L2, slide 36: Many or an unknown number of parallel hierarchies "get out of hand"; the information becomes scattered.

name: Which statements about the Accountability pattern (Party, Accountability, AccountabilityType, TimePeriod) are correct?

answers.body: Its links connect only organisational units, so a driver cannot take part in one.
answers.comment: L2, slides 39–41: People have similar relationships to organisations or other people; Party covers both.

answers.body: Each Accountability links exactly two parties (commissioner and responsible); its AccountabilityType says what kind of link it is.
answers.comment: L2, slide 39: Each instance links two parties; the type indicates the nature of the link, so any number of relationship kinds can be handled.

answers.body: It reuses the recursive association of Organization Hierarchies, so no link objects are needed.
answers.comment: L2, slide 39: It combines Party with the principle of Organization Structure, where links are objects, not plain associations.

answers.body: A TimePeriod attached to an Accountability can record when a responsibility was valid.
answers.comment: L2, slides 39 and 48: TimePeriod is an example of context on the accountability, answering "temporary or permanent, is history needed?"

name: In the Accountability Knowledge Level pattern, what does a ConnectionRule describe?

answers.body: Part of the configuration above the operational level, which every operational Accountability must respect.
answers.comment: L2, slide 42: The knowledge level is the configuration of the operational level.

answers.body: A replacement for the two Party ends of an operational Accountability, so that accountabilities no longer need to link parties.
answers.comment: L2, slides 42–43: Each Accountability still links its two parties; rules only say which party types may be linked.

answers.body: The concrete people and depots that take part in one particular assignment, e.g. driver Novák at Depot North.
answers.comment: L2, slide 42: Concrete participants are Party objects at the operational level; rules speak about types.

answers.body: One legal pairing of parent and child PartyTypes for a given AccountabilityType, e.g. driver → assignment to workplace → depot.
answers.comment: L2, slides 42–43: Each accountability type has a group of connection rules, each defining one legal parent/child party-type pairing.

name: During requirements analysis a new role (e.g. Inspector) is discovered. What does the separation of knowledge level and operational level give you?

answers.body: Every concrete Party is replaced by a ConnectionRule, so the operational level disappears.
answers.comment: L2, slide 44: The two levels keep their meanings; parties remain operational objects.

answers.body: A flexible way to discuss roles and their relationships with stakeholders.
answers.comment: L2, slide 44: The knowledge level drives discussion about roles and their relationships and gives flexibility.

answers.body: Roles no longer need to be clarified with stakeholders.
answers.comment: L2, slide 44: The pattern supports the discussion of roles; it does not replace it.

answers.body: Only the knowledge-level specifications change; the operational level stays untouched as a stable backbone.
answers.comment: L2, slide 44: "Nothing" happens: the knowledge level is updated and the operational level is untouched.

name: How does the Accountability knowledge level relate to authorization?

answers.body: Discussing user roles and responsibilities is in effect discussing authorization; connection rules are often authorization rules.
answers.comment: L2, slide 45: A role accountable for something must be authorized to do it, so connection rules often are authorization rules.

answers.body: Authorization rules mainly need explicit clarification in multi-tenant systems such as GitHub.
answers.comment: L2, slide 45: Authorization must be clarified explicitly in any modern system.

answers.body: The conceptual model fixes one authorization technology, so RBAC or ABAC is chosen before analysis begins.
answers.comment: L2, slide 45: The mental model captures authorization principles regardless of technology.

answers.body: The operational realization can be role-based or attribute-based access control.
answers.comment: L2, slide 45: RBAC and ABAC are given as possible realizations of the operational level.

name: Stakeholders are asked: "What happens when the company adds a new role next year? Who configures authorization, and when?" How does the answer affect the system boundary?

answers.body: Both answers lead to the same implemented functionality and the same system boundary.
answers.comment: L2, slide 46: The answers differ in whether the knowledge level is part of the system.

answers.body: Independent per-tenant configuration (as in multi-tenant systems) can be achieved with hard-coded if-else branches alone.
answers.comment: L2, slide 46: Dynamic, independent configurability of tenants is the typical case for implementing the knowledge level as data.

answers.body: If developers adapt the system in a new version, the knowledge level serves only as rules for implementation (new if-else branches).
answers.comment: L2, slide 46: With developer-made changes, the knowledge level stays a blueprint for the code.

answers.body: If a user must add roles from the UI, the knowledge level has to be implemented too, and the running system only changes data.
answers.comment: L2, slide 46: Runtime configuration requires implemented accountability types, party types and connection rules.

name: In a transport company, (1) the right to approve drivers' overtime belongs to the position "depot manager" and must not change when a new person takes the job, and (2) the knowledge level repeats the same connection rules for Driver, Technician and Dispatcher, which is getting hard to maintain. Which further Accountability patterns address these needs?

answers.body: (1) Attach the approval right to the current person and copy it whenever the holder changes.
answers.comment: L2, slides 47–48: "Is responsibility tied to the person or to the post?" – here it is tied to the post, so Post avoids copying.

answers.body: (2) Party Type Generalization: introduce a general party type (e.g. Employee) so one rule covers its subtypes.
answers.comment: L2, slide 47: Adding generalization to party types makes the knowledge level easier to define.

answers.body: (2) Hierarchic Accountability: it records which person currently holds which post, so rules apply per holder.
answers.comment: L2, slide 47: Hierarchic Accountability improves handling of constraints in organisation structures; it does not track post holders.

answers.body: (1) Post: model the position as another party type that holds the accountability, separate from the person occupying it.
answers.comment: L2, slide 47: Posts are used when accountability and scopes are defined by the post and do not change when the holder changes.

name: Sketch a conceptual UML class model for a public transport company. A dispatcher creates daily work schedules; a daily work schedule refers to a line, and each line has its line schedule. A daily work schedule is assigned to drivers. Drivers can be licensed for vehicles independently of which vehicle they currently drive; vehicles are buses, trams and trolleybuses. Then list the requirements questions you must ask before fixing the multiplicities and history of the driving relationship and of vehicle records.
answer:
Entities. Dispatcher, DailyWorkSchedule, Line, LineSchedule, Driver and Vehicle, with Bus, Tram and TrolleyBus as subclasses of Vehicle.
Associations. Dispatcher –creates→ DailyWorkSchedule; DailyWorkSchedule – Line; Line – LineSchedule (keep the two schedule concepts distinct); DailyWorkSchedule – Driver. Between Driver and Vehicle draw two separate associations: has licence (many-to-many) and drives, whose multiplicity stays provisional.
Questions about the driving relationship. When is a driver assigned to a vehicle? Does the driver take the first free tram of the line, or does each driver have "his" vehicle shared with others in turns? How permanent is the assignment? What must be remembered about it, and who is responsible for that information?
Questions about vehicle records. Who manages vehicle records? What is the process of taking a vehicle out of service, and is it inside the system boundary? If a vehicle is put out of service, should its history be kept?
Draw conceptual entities only: no methods, no database keys.
keyPoints: Includes the stated concepts, with Bus, Tram and TrolleyBus as Vehicle subclasses.
Links DailyWorkSchedule to Line and Line to LineSchedule, keeping the two schedules distinct.
Separates "has licence" from "drives" between Driver and Vehicle.
Names associations and marks the driving multiplicity as provisional until clarified.
Asks about timing, permanence and history of driving assignments and who is responsible for them.
Asks who manages vehicle records and whether out-of-service handling and its history are inside the system boundary.
source: 02-03-Analysis-patterns.pdf, slides 8–10 (entities, relationships and the transport conceptual model with its context and class questions); public-transport.pdf, pages 2–3.

name: Model the following description with the Organization Hierarchies pattern: "Dispatchers sit at headquarters. Technicians and drivers are located at their depot. Headquarters manages depots." First give the straightforward model with one association per relationship, then the pattern-based model, and say where the rules go.
answer:
Straightforward model. Headquarter 1 – * Depot; Headquarter 1 – * Dispatcher; Depot 1 – * Technician; Depot 1 – * Driver. Each relationship is a separate association, so any new unit or level changes the schema ("you get what you ask for").
Pattern-based model. One abstract class OrganizationUnit with a recursive association: parent (0..1) and subsidiaries (*). Subclasses: Headquarter, Depot, HqEmployee (with subclass Dispatcher) and DepotEmployee (with subclasses Technician and Driver).
Rules. Constraints are attached to subclasses: the parent of an HqEmployee is a Headquarter; the parent of a DepotEmployee is a Depot; the parent of a Depot is a Headquarter.
Trade-off. The pattern version is more complex but flexible: a new kind of unit is a new subclass plus a rule, not new associations. The top unit needs a parent multiplicity of 0..1 so it can exist without a parent.
keyPoints: Straightforward model has separate associations Headquarter–Depot, Headquarter–Dispatcher, Depot–Technician and Depot–Driver.
Pattern model uses one OrganizationUnit class with a recursive parent/subsidiary association.
Headquarter, Depot and the employee kinds are subclasses, with grouping such as HqEmployee and DepotEmployee.
Parent rules (e.g. parent = Depot for depot employees) are constraints on the subclasses.
Explains the trade-off: more complex, but new units need a subclass and a rule rather than a schema change; root parent 0..1.
source: 02-03-Analysis-patterns.pdf, slides 28–34 (Organization Hierarchies; transport example on slide 34). The slide 34 diagram shows parent multiplicity 1 at the top; the 0..1 remark follows the generic pattern on slide 30 and the silent-incompleteness example on slide 18.

name: Draw a UML class fragment and an object example for two simultaneous structures. In Sale, the Brno sales office reports to the Moravia division and the Prague sales office to the Bohemia division. In PublicRelations, both offices report to the Central operating unit. Use the Organization Structure pattern so that the offices are shared between the two structures.
answer:
Classes. OrganizationStructureType; OrganizationStructure, each with one type and two Organization ends named parent and subsidiary; Organization with subclasses SalesOffice, Division and OperatingUnit.
Objects. Organizations Brno and Prague (SalesOffice), Moravia and Bohemia (Division), Central (OperatingUnit). Type objects Sale and PublicRelations.
Links (four OrganizationStructure objects).
Sale:            parent = Moravia,  subsidiary = Brno
Sale:            parent = Bohemia,  subsidiary = Prague
PublicRelations: parent = Central,  subsidiary = Brno
PublicRelations: parent = Central,  subsidiary = Prague
Brno and Prague are the same objects in both structures. Rules per structure type (e.g. "in Sale, a SalesOffice reports to a Division") are attached to the type or the subclasses, rather than requiring one parent across both structures. Each structure object can also carry context such as a TimePeriod.
keyPoints: Reifies each typed parent–subsidiary relationship as an OrganizationStructure object.
Sale and PublicRelations are instances of OrganizationStructureType, not new classes or associations.
The same Brno and Prague objects appear in both structures.
Shows all four links with the right parents and types.
Keeps type-specific rules and extra context (e.g. TimePeriod) explicit.
source: 02-03-Analysis-patterns.pdf, slides 35–38 (Multiple Organization Hierarchies, Organization Structure and its exercise); public-transport.pdf, page 5.

name: Extend a public transport responsibility model with Party, Accountability and a knowledge level. Requirements: a driver may be temporarily assigned to a second depot, and an accident investigation must find which assignments were valid at the accident time. Use this orientation for workplace assignment: the employee is the parent and the depot is the child; for work distribution the distributor is the parent and the worker the child. Show the knowledge-level party types, accountability types and the connection rules for Driver–Depot and Technician–Depot workplace assignment and for Dispatcher–Driver and DepotManager–Technician work distribution. Show one example of operational objects.
answer:
Operational level. Party (with concrete parties such as driver Novák, Depot North, Depot South) and Accountability. Each Accountability has two Party ends (parent and child), one AccountabilityType and a TimePeriod.
Knowledge level. PartyType instances: Driver, Technician, Dispatcher, DepotManager, Depot. AccountabilityType instances: WorkplaceAssignment and WorkDistribution. Each Party has one PartyType. Each AccountabilityType has ConnectionRules with an allowed parent and an allowed child PartyType:
WorkplaceAssignment: (Driver, Depot), (Technician, Depot)
WorkDistribution:    (Dispatcher, Driver), (DepotManager, Technician)
Temporary second depot. Store it as another WorkplaceAssignment Accountability (Novák → Depot South) with its own TimePeriod, next to the permanent one (Novák → Depot North). Nothing is overwritten. To answer the accident question, select the accountabilities whose TimePeriod contains the accident time.
Open questions. Are the connection rules maintained by developers or configured by users through the UI (system boundary)? These rules also express authorization.
keyPoints: Separates knowledge-level PartyType, AccountabilityType and ConnectionRule from operational Party and Accountability.
Each Accountability has two Party ends, one type and a TimePeriod.
Lists all four connection rules with the stated parent–child orientation.
Records the temporary assignment as an additional dated Accountability instead of overwriting the depot.
Answers the accident question by selecting accountabilities valid at that time.
Raises who maintains the rules (developers vs. UI) and their link to authorization.
source: 02-03-Analysis-patterns.pdf, slides 16 and 39–48 (temporary second-depot requirement, Accountability, Knowledge Level with the connection rules on slide 43, authorization and system boundary); public-transport.pdf, pages 6–8. The example parties are invented for illustration.

name: Test a model with instances. An LLM produced this model for a coffee-machine company: class Organization with a recursive association, <TT>parent</TT> multiplicity 1 and <TT>children</TT> multiplicity *. Requirements from the brief: (R1) Associated Coffee Makers is the top organisation; (R2) its departments are sales and purchasing; (R3) sales has offices in Boston and London. Build an object diagram for these requirements, say which requirement cannot be instantiated and why, and propose the fix.
answer:
Object diagram. Objects: acm : Organization (Associated Coffee Makers), sales : Organization, purchasing : Organization, boston : Organization, london : Organization. Links: sales.parent = acm, purchasing.parent = acm, boston.parent = sales, london.parent = sales.
Gap. R1 cannot be instantiated: multiplicity 1 forces acm to have a parent, but by definition the top organisation has none. To satisfy the model you would have to invent an extra anonymous Organization above acm, which is wrong. R2 and R3 work.
Fix. Change parent to 0..1, so exactly one organisation (the root) may lack a parent.
Lesson. This is silent incompleteness: the model looks confident and raises no error. No pattern fixes it; only writing down requirements and trying to build instances reveals it.
keyPoints: Builds instances acm, sales, purchasing, boston and london with the correct parent links.
Identifies R1 (the top organisation) as the requirement that cannot be instantiated.
Explains that multiplicity 1 forces every Organization, including the root, to have a parent.
Proposes parent multiplicity 0..1.
Names this as silent incompleteness, found by testing with instances rather than by reading.
source: 02-03-Analysis-patterns.pdf, slide 18 (silent incompleteness, Organization with parent 1 and the crossed-out extra parent object); slide 30 uses parent 0..1.
